Netflix's cloud migration story is one of the most famous case study in tech. In August 2008 Netflix experienced a massive database corruption in its on-premises Oracle database. This affected the DVD rental business, making it impossible for Netflix to ship DVDs to customers for three days. The incident exposed the limitations of traditional on-premises infrastructure. Netflix realized it needed a highly scalable, fault-tolerant, and globally distributed system that could withstand failures. After evaluating different options, Netflix decided to move its entire IT infrastructure to Amazon Web Services. This doesn't just help Netflix with scalability, global reach and fault tolerance but also with cost reduction. Their cloud costs per streaming start ended up being a fraction of those in the data center. #dataanalytics #dataengineering #data

* 🎬 Ever paused a Netflix show halfway and picked it up later — even on another device? That seamless “Continue Watching” experience is something we all love. Out of Netflix’s 300+ million users, anyone can resume exactly where they left off — and even see a feed of everything they stopped midway. But have you ever wondered how this actually works behind the scenes? ⚙️ 1. The Client Tracks and Reports Progress As you watch, your app keeps track of how many seconds you’ve completed. But this info needs to live in the cloud, not just on your phone — so you can continue on any device. However, sending an update every second would flood Netflix’s servers. So instead, the app sends progress updates only at key points — when you pause, stop, skip, or close the app. 🚫 2. Why Direct Database Writes Don’t Scale A naïve approach would be: every update writes directly to the main user database. At Netflix scale, that would mean millions of writes per second — instant chaos. Databases would choke, causing slowdowns or outages. 📨 3. Introducing Asynchronous Messaging To handle this load, Netflix decouples the write path. Instead of writing to the database immediately, the app sends a small message to a message queue (think Kafka or AWS Kinesis). The queue instantly acknowledges the message — so the app stays fast and responsive. 🧩 4. Batch Processing in the Background Backend workers process messages from the queue in batches or near real-time, updating each user’s watch position. Batching keeps things efficient, reduces write pressure, and ensures resilience — even if a server fails, messages aren’t lost. 💡 This design makes the “Continue Watching” feature feel effortless — but behind it is a highly optimized, distributed system built for scale, resilience, and real-time user delight. #Netflix #SystemDesign #DataEngineering #Scalability #TechArchitecture #HLD #Cloud

* "Uffff the doubt has been clarified! 😮 I always wondered how Netflix streams movies even if I’m in a remote area with no data center nearby. The answer is Content Delivery Networks (CDNs) + caching..." 🌍 Problem: If you are in a remote area or country with no Netflix data center nearby, how does Netflix still stream movies with low buffering and high quality? 🚀 The Solution: CDNs (Content Delivery Networks) + Caching Data Centers are not everywhere Big tech companies (Netflix, YouTube, Amazon, etc.) don’t put full data centers in every city — that’s too expensive. Instead, they rely on CDNs. CDNs (Content Delivery Networks) Netflix uses its own CDN called Open Connect. A CDN is a global network of cache servers placed in many ISPs (like Airtel, Jio, Comcast) and at the edge of the internet. These CDN servers store copies of popular movies, shows, trailers, etc. 👉 Example: If 1 million people in India watch Money Heist, Netflix caches it on Indian CDN servers. When you click play, the video comes from a nearby CDN (maybe in your ISP’s local server) instead of from the US. If No Local CDN Nearby? Netflix still streams content, but your request may be routed to the nearest CDN available (maybe in the nearest country/region). Advanced protocols + compression + adaptive bitrate ensure you still get smooth streaming. 👉 Example: If you’re in a very remote area with no ISP CDN, your request might hit a regional hub (like Singapore, Dubai, or Frankfurt) depending on routing. Adaptive Bitrate Streaming Netflix dynamically adjusts quality: If the nearest CDN is far → lower quality but still streams. If nearby CDN is available → high quality (4K). This is why sometimes quality auto-adjusts when your network fluctuates. 🔑 Real-Time Flow (When You Hit “Play”) Netflix App → Asks Netflix servers which CDN node is closest to you. Netflix → Redirects your video stream request to that CDN. CDN → Streams cached content (movie/show). If not cached → CDN pulls it once from the main Netflix data center → stores it locally → serves it to you and future viewers. ⚡ Why This Works Amazingly CDNs are geographically distributed, so even if Netflix has 30 data centers worldwide, it has thousands of CDN edge servers closer to users. That’s how they can serve millions of requests per second globally. ✅ So even if you’re in a remote area, Netflix doesn’t need to build a data center near you — it relies on CDNs + ISPs caching to deliver the movie.

* Recently, while going through the Netflix newsletter, I came across a blog about how Netflix is shifting from its traditional infrastructure to a hybrid approach — combining serverless (AWS Lambdas) with traditional methods — to reduce cost and operational effort. This really caught my attention because it reflects a much broader trend we’re seeing across the IT industry. More and more companies are realizing that a “serverless-only” or “traditional-only” strategy doesn’t always fit every workload. Netflix’s example shows how hybrid architectures can offer the best of both worlds: Serverless for event-driven, short-lived, or automated tasks (like log processing and scaling microservices) Traditional or container-based setups for heavy, long-running workloads (like video transcoding or data streaming) In my latest vlog, I break down this hybrid approach and discuss: ✅ Why companies like Netflix are moving toward serverless ✅ When serverless is (and isn’t) the right choice ✅ Real-world examples of cost savings and performance gains ✅ The future of “serverless-first” architectures If you’re exploring cloud optimization or thinking about how serverless fits into your system design, this one’s worth a watch. 🎥 Check out my new vlog: https://lnkd.in/d4XcEGBw Would love to hear — do you see serverless becoming a bigger part of your tech stack, or do you think hybrid is the smarter way forward?

* Everyone talks about Netflix, Amazon, and Uber when they explain microservices. But here’s the truth: → You are not Netflix. → You don’t have thousands of engineers. → You don’t need a hundred microservices to ship value. Netflix moved to microservices because streaming at global scale broke their monolith. Amazon broke apart their system because one giant codebase slowed down independent teams. Uber scaled microservices because they had to manage real-time rides across the world. For most companies, a monolith can carry you a very long way. It’s easier, faster, and less expensive. Microservices only become relevant when: → Teams are too big to move inside one codebase. → Features need to ship independently. → Scaling is required at a global level. The real lesson? Don’t copy Netflix just because it sounds cool. Choose based on your stage, not the hype. 🚀 👉 If you had to start your company’s architecture today, would you go monolith first or microservices from day one?

* 🚨 How Netflix Survived the AWS Cloud Outage!! Most people think Netflix just got lucky. They didn’t. Netflix expects the cloud to fail — and designs for it before it happens. That mindset is what separates resilience from downtime. Here’s why Netflix stayed up even when AWS didn’t 👇 ✅ Cached Authentication: IAM/STS tokens are cached — so user sessions don’t need to re-authenticate mid-playback. ✅ Local Config & Edge Loading: App configurations are loaded locally or from edge nodes, not fetched live from AWS during requests. ✅ Pre-Pulled Container Images: All container images are already pulled and ready — no dependency on ECR when AWS control-plane goes down. ✅ Minimal Runtime Dependencies: The runtime avoids frequent network metadata lookups, preventing throttling from AWS control-plane failures. 📌 In short: Netflix doesn’t rely on AWS being “healthy” at runtime. They shrink their live dependencies on the cloud control-plane — and that’s the real definition of resilience. #AWS #CloudComputing #Resilience #Netflix #DevOps #SRE

* 🎬 A bold strategic paradox: Netflix runs on Amazon’s cloud. While Netflix and Amazon Prime Video compete fiercely in the streaming industry, Netflix chose to host its entire platform on Amazon Web Services (AWS)- the cloud arm of its biggest rival. Why? Because strategy isn’t just about competition- it’s about capability. Netflix understood that AWS offered unmatched scalability, reliability, and innovation speed, enabling it to deliver seamless streaming to millions of users worldwide. This move perfectly illustrates the modern concept of “coopetition”- where competitors collaborate when it creates mutual strategic value. Netflix prioritized growth, agility, and customer experience over rivalry, proving that smart partnerships drive innovation. “In today’s economy, strategic success lies in choosing what enables growth, not just who you compete against.” #DigitalTransformation #Strategy #AWS #Netflix #Innovation #CloudComputing #Leadership #Coopetition #BusinessStrategy #CareerGrowth #DCU #Employer #Business #Dublin

* 🎬 How Netflix Streams Millions of Shows Seamlessly ? Ever wondered how Netflix manages to stream billions of hours without hiccups? It’s not magic — it’s engineering at scale. Netflix uses edge servers close to users so videos start instantly, no matter where you are. Behind the scenes, it runs thousands of microservices, each handling a different part of the system — from user accounts, search, and playback, to recommendations and billing. This architecture allows Netflix to deploy updates quickly without taking down the whole platform. All of this lives on the cloud, which can scale up or down automatically when millions of people hit “play” at the same time. Machine learning powers the personalized suggestions you see (“Because you watched…”), while tools like Chaos Monkey intentionally break parts of the system to make sure it stays reliable. Netflix also optimizes video quality using adaptive streaming, so your show plays smoothly even on slower internet connections. And it constantly collects data on viewing habits, which feeds into improving recommendations, content delivery, and system efficiency. Takeaway: Netflix is a masterclass in applying core computer science concepts — data, networks, storage, cloud, and resilience — to real-world systems at massive scale. All so that users across the globe can have fun Binge Watching without any major interruptions. Netflix's beauty is at it's core engineering tech principles applied at scale. #SystemDesign #Netflix #SoftwareEngineering #DistributedSystems #Cloud #TechStory #CaseStudy

* How Netflix optimized AWS costs without compromising performance When you serve 300+ million users worldwide, performance is the key. Netflix faced a classic scaling challenge of keeping streaming fast, reliable and global, while cloud costs kept rising. Instead of just cutting resources, Netflix re-engineered its AWS architecture: 1) Adopted microservices to achieve better scalability and fault isolation 2) Leveraged AWS EC2, S3, and CloudFront for elastic compute, efficient storage, and low-latency content delivery 3) Implemented cost guardrails, real-time efficiency metrics, and workload tuning to match demand dynamically 4) Optimized data pipelines and autoscaling strategies to balance cost with peak performance As a result, Netflix saved billions in AWS spend while maintaining top-tier streaming performance across regions. Performance optimization isn’t only about code speed, it’s about cloud efficiency, architecture choices and giving teams the right data to make smart trade-offs.
